title: Green Bonds as Hedging and Safe-Haven Assets: Evidence from Equity–Bond Co-Movements in Small Open Economies during COVID-19 and the Russia–Ukraine Crisis

p.t: Green bonds have become a salient segment of sustainable finance, channeling capital to renewable energy, clean transport, and other environmental projects. Market growth has been rapid over the past decade, supported by rising institutional demand and policy initiatives (Climate Bonds Initiative, 2023;Flammer, 2021;Zerbib, 2019;Larcker & Watts, 2020). Outstanding green-bond volumes surpassed USD 1.5 trillion by mid-2023, signaling wider adoption across sovereign, supranational, and corporate issuers as Environmental, Social, Governance (ESG henceforward) moved into the mainstream (Climate Bonds Initiative, 2023). While pricing research documents a modest and context-dependent "greenium" (Zerbib, 2019;Larcker & Watts, 2020;Flammer, 2021), less is known about the risk role of green bonds in, highly developed Small Open Economies (SOEs) markets. We examine twelve highly developed Small Open Economies (SOEs) countries using daily price-index equity returns and a global green bond index over 2014-2023. The sample is characterized as a mix of highly developed small open economies (SOEs) and advanced European non-G20 markets that rely heavily on global capital channels. The analysis focuses on two portfolio-relevant properties. The first one is whether green bonds help reduce routine equity risk in tranquil periods (hedging), and the other one is whether their co-movement weakens or turns negative under acute stress (safe-haven behavior). We implement fixed-effects panel regressions with crisis interactions for the COVID-19 pandemic, from 11 March 2020, and the Russia-Ukraine war, from 24 February 2022. We verify country heterogeneity through country-level OLS robustness checks with HAC (Newey-West) errors to accommodate serial correlation in daily data (Newey & West, 1987). In doing so, we extend evidence beyond large advanced economies to markets whose depth, liquidity, and policy frameworks can yield materially different cross-asset dynamics (Baur & Lucey, 2010;Baur & McDermott, 2010;Reboredo, 2018). This analysis develops country-specific evidence for twelve highly developed Small Open Economies (SOEs) markets, clarifying where green bonds deliver diversification in calm conditions. It then estimates crisis-contingent shifts by interacting green-bond returns with the COVID-19 and Russia-Ukraine windows, thereby separating routine hedging from behavior under stress. Finally, it evaluates reliability by varying the COVID-19 onset (11 March vs. 1 February 2020) and re-estimating at the country level with HAC (Newey-West) errors, ensuring that the main results do not hinge on pooled specifications or a single crisis date.

p.s: Green Bonds: Historical Development, Economic Significance, and Financial Market Linkages
p.t: Green bonds, also referred to as climate bonds, are fixed-income securities whose proceeds are earmarked for projects with positive environmental impact-such as renewable energy, energy efficiency, low-carbon transport, sustainable water management, and pollution reduction (Ferrer, Shahzad, & Soriano, 2021;Reboredo, 2018). The first green bond-issued by the European Investment Bank in 2007 as a "climate awareness bond"-is widely viewed as the market's inception point (Ferrer et al., 2021). Subsequent growth accelerated after the publication of the Green Bond Principles by the International Capital Markets Association in 2014, which introduced voluntary process guidelines for use-of-proceeds, project evaluation, management of proceeds, and reporting, fostering labeling consistency and transparency (Ferrer et al., 2021;Reboredo & Ugolini, 2020). The creation of dedicated green-bond segments on several exchanges (e.g., Italy, Norway, the U.K., Mexico, Luxembourg, China) further supported market visibility and secondary-market development (Ferrer et al., 2021). Empirical evidence indicates that green bonds are closely linked to government and investment-grade corporate bonds, reflecting similar duration, credit quality, and pricing mechanics (Ferrer et al., 2021;Reboredo, 2018;Reboredo & Ugolini, 2020). In contrast, linkages with equities, renewable-energy stocks, and crude oil tend to be limited across horizons, and shock transmission appears predominantly short-lived, it is often less than five trading days, suggesting transitory spillovers rather than persistent co-movement (Ferrer et al., 2021). These patterns are consistent with the view that green bonds do not constitute a distinct asset class but largely behave like high-quality fixed income while still offering scope for diversification and risk mitigation (Ferrer et al., 2021;Reboredo, 2018).

p.s: Green Bonds: Historical Development, Economic Significance, and Financial Market Linkages
p.t: Α well-specified ESG fixed-income sleeve, with labelled green bonds at its core, broadens the investable sustainable universe, facilitates mandate compliance, and can lower tracking error relative to ESG benchmarks while preserving diversification against equity risk. In highly developed Small Open Economies (SOEs) markets, where local issuance and secondary-market depth are often limited, global or regional green-bond indices become the practical conduit for ESG integration, with implications for currency management, liquidity costs, and benchmark composition risk. Credible standards and certification (ICMA Green Bond Principles; Climate Bonds Initiative) support this portfolio role by mitigating greenwashing and sustaining investor demand, which the literature links to pricing premia, the "greenium" and persistent capital allocation toward greener assets (Zerbib, 2019;Larcker & Watts, 2020;Flammer, 2021). Accordingly, the ESG portfolio context helps explain both the scaling potential of green bonds and the state-contingent nature of their risk properties documented here, complementing climate policy and the development of a more sustainable financial system (Ferrer, Shahzad, & Soriano, 2021;Reboredo & Ugolini, 2020).

In asset allocation, a hedge is understood as an asset held continuously to attenuate ordinary fluctuations in a reference exposure or portfolio. Conceptually, a hedge contributes diversification by offsetting or diluting the systematic risks embedded in the target position through distinct cash-flow characteristics, risk premia, and investor clientele. Its role is evaluated unconditionally, on normal market states, and its contribution is to reduce variance and improve risk-adjusted performance in routine conditions, notably without requiring market timing. A safe haven is an asset expected to preserve or increase value specifically during acute stress, serving as a state-contingent insurance against tail losses. The defining feature here is conditionality. A safe haven is not required to protect portfolios in tranquil periods. Its defining attribute is zero or negative co-movement with the target, specifically during crises, thereby mitigating drawdowns precisely when cross-asset correlations tend to spike. (Baur & Lucey, 2010;Reboredo, 2018;Ferrer, Shahzad, & Soriano, 2021). In economic terms, safe-haven behavior is associated with attributes that attract capital in turmoil-perceived safety of cash flows (e.g., high-grade sovereign backing), deep and resilient liquidity, collateral eligibility, or convention as a store of value-so that during dislocations investors rotate into the asset rather than away from it (Baur & Lucey, 2010;Baur & McDermott, 2010). Sustainable-finance studies adopt this state-contingent taxonomy when assessing labeled green bonds and, for comparison, ESG equities, asking whether these instruments provide routine diversification (hedge) and/or crisis-time capital preservation (safe haven) across markets and episodes (Reboredo, 2018;Ferrer et al., 2021;Naeem et al., 2021;Umar et al., 2022;Piserà & Chiappini, 2024).

Evidence places green bonds close to high-quality sovereign and investment-grade corporate debt in duration and credit characteristics, which supports equity diversification in tranquil periods (Reboredo, 2018;Ferrer et al., 2021;Reboredo & Ugolini, 2020). Their crisis-time behavior, however, varies across episodes and markets. Temporary decoupling has been documented under severe stress, yet in other cases co-movement does not fall-as liquidity constraints, flight-to-quality into the safest government debt, and demand shocks in labeled fixed income can synchronize returns with broader risk repricing (Ferrer et al., 2021;Naeem et al., 2021a). These mechanisms imply that green bonds can behave as partial, context-dependent hedges and only occasionally as safe havens, depending on the nature of the shock and market microstructure. Highly developed Small Open Economies (SOEs) markets typically display thinner secondary-market liquidity, a more concentrated investor base, and heterogeneous disclosure/certification practices for labeled debt. Such features amplify cross-country variation in the transmission of global shocks and in the degree to which green bonds align with local sovereign benchmarks versus global credit. Consequently, a pooled average can conceal meaningful country heterogeneity, reinforcing the need for market-by-market assessment in addition to pooled inference.

p.s: The Greenium and the Risk of Greenwashing
p.t: The concept of the greenium (a combination of green and premium) has become central to the study of sustainable finance. It refers to the yield differential between green bonds and comparable conventional bonds issued by the same entity, with green bonds often priced at a lower yield. This implies that issuers of green bonds can obtain financing at a reduced cost, while investors demonstrate a willingness to sacrifice part of their financial return in exchange for environmental benefits and alignment with ESG criteria (Zerbib, 2019). Early empirical research demonstrated that this pricing anomaly is linked to investors' pro-environmental preferences, showing that the demand for green assets creates measurable effects in bond markets (Zerbib, 2019). More recent studies have examined the dynamics of the greenium in different contexts and timeframes. For instance, Pietsch and Salakhova (2025) analyzed euro area markets between 2016 and 2023 and found that the greenium, while relatively small, is statistically significant. Their results suggest that retail investor demand plays a crucial role in amplifying or reducing the greenium across time, highlighting the importance of investor composition in sustainable finance. Regional perspectives also provide insights into the credibility of the greenium. Dryden and Pulieri (2025), focusing on Asian green bond markets, argue that certification and trust in the "greenness" of bonds directly influence the magnitude of the greenium. They caution, however, that the risk of greenwashing-the misrepresentation of environmental benefits-can undermine this premium, suggesting that the persistence of the greenium depends heavily on transparent standards and governance structures. Similarly, Wang and Xia (2023) contend that prior research may have underestimated the greenium due to the so-called "green halo effect," where conventional bonds issued by frequent green bond issuers also benefit indirectly from investors' environmental preferences. Their findings indicate that the greenium is both statistically and economically significant, not only at issuance but also in secondary markets, reinforcing the idea that sustainability preferences are embedded in financial pricing mechanisms. A further challenge linked to the persistence of the greenium is the risk of greenwashing. Greenwashing occurs when financial instruments are marketed as environmentally friendly without delivering meaningful or verifiable environmental benefits. In the context of green bonds, this misrepresentation undermines investor trust and can distort the measurement of the greenium, as investors may inadvertently pay a premium for projects that do not genuinely advance sustainability goals. Dryden and Pulieri (2025) emphasize that the credibility of the greenium in Asia depends heavily on robust certification processes and transparent reporting standards, which help protect markets from greenwashing. Without stringent oversight and accountability, the greenium risks become a reflection not of true environmental value but of superficial labeling, weakening both investor confidence and the broader objectives of sustainable finance. Overall, literature converges on the view that greenium represents a structural shift in capital allocation, where environmental considerations are internalized into financial decision-making. While the magnitude of the greenium varies across markets, time periods, and regulatory frameworks, it consistently demonstrates that sustainability preferences have tangible economic effects in global bond markets

An ESG portfolio is an investment construct that integrates environmental, social, and governance information into security selection, portfolio construction, and risk control with a dual aim: competitive risk-adjusted returns and alignment with clearly articulated sustainability objectives. In this context, ESG does not denote a single score or a moral screen; it is a framework for identifying channels through which environmental constraints, social practices, and governance quality can affect cash flows, discount rates, tail risks, and ultimately the co-movement of assets within a diversified portfolio. In fixed income, this framework is applied both to conventional "unlabeled" bonds-where ESG variables are incorporated in valuation and risk models-and to "labelled" instruments, most prominently green bonds, whose proceeds are earmarked for environmentally beneficial projects under recognized market standards such as the ICMA Green Bond Principles, which codify use-of-proceeds, project evaluation and selection, management of proceeds, and annual impact reporting (ICMA, 2018(ICMA, /2021)). The institutionalization of these principles, together with external reviews and Climate Bonds Initiative certification, aims to mitigate greenwashing and to support investor confidence and secondary-market liquidity, both of which are relevant for the asset's risk behavior (Climate Bonds Initiative, 2023; Reboredo & Ugolini, 2020). The economic rationale for ESG integration rests on financially material channels. Transition risk-arising from carbon pricing, regulation, technological substitution, and shifting demand-can reshape margins and capital expenditure paths for high-emitting issuers and therefore alter default probabilities and credit spreads in bonds and valuation multiples in equities (Bolton & Kacperczyk, 2021). Physical risk-acute events such as storms and floods, and chronic pressures such as heat and water stress-can impair assets and supply chains, increasing earnings volatility and financing needs. Governance and social frictions-board effectiveness, shareholder rights, audit quality, labor and product-safety practices-shape agency costs and event risk. These channels map directly into bond-market quantities (spread levels and volatility, liquidity premia, duration profiles) and into equity metrics (beta, profitability persistence, drawdowns). Empirically, ESG issues have been associated with future profitability and lower risk at the firm level, while meta-evidence suggests that ESG integration is at least non-detrimental to performance on average and often improves downside protection, particularly in diversified portfolios (Friede, Busch, & Bassen, 2015;Khan, Serafeim, & Yoon, 2016). Previous research investigated whether investors pay a "greenium", finding effects that are small but often statistically significant (Zerbib, 2019;Larcker & Watts, 2020;Flammer, 2021). From a portfolio perspective, the presence of a greenium implies a potential trade-off between expected return and ancillary benefits such as lower volatility, drawdown mitigation, mandate compliance, and measurable project impacts. The present study investigates if green bonds diversify equity risk in normal conditions and whether they protect capital in crises.

The differences between an asset held as a hedge and one perceived as safe haven reflect differences in underlying cash flows, risk premia, and liquidity regimes that drive state-contingent investor flows. In calm periods, high-grade, duration-bearing bonds-green bonds included-are economically distinct from equity cash-flow risk and therefore natural candidates to hedge equity exposure. In dislocations, however, funding and market-liquidity stress can compress distinctions between risky assets and credit-like instruments, potentially tightening co-movement and attenuating safe-haven properties. The literature on green bonds is consistent with this state-contingent view: correlations with equities are generally low in tranquil periods, but crisis behavior is heterogeneous across markets and episodes, reflecting benchmark composition (credit-spread versus duration tilt), market depth, and the investor base (Reboredo, 2018;Ferrer, Shahzad, & Soriano, 2021;Reboredo & Ugolini, 2020). While the expanding body of sustainable finance literature has established that green bonds share close risk characteristics with traditional corporate investment-grade fixed income (Reboredo, 2018;Ferrer et al., 2021), a glaring omission persists regarding how these dynamics manifest across diverse market regimes within highly developed Small Open Economies (SOEs). Existing studies heavily lean toward large, systemic G20 markets (e.g., the US, Eurozone, and China), leaving a theoretical vacuum on how state-contingent co-movements behave in countries that are highly financially integrated but structurally dependent on global liquidity currents (Lane & Milesi-Ferretti, 2007). Furthermore, the literature frequently treats 'crisis' as a uniform state, overlooking the distinct transmission mechanisms of public health shocks versus geopolitical conflicts. This paper directly addresses these gaps by evaluating whether global green bond allocations offer autonomous localized insulation when structural asset relationships fracture under distinct global stress regimes highly developed Small Open Economies (SOEs)The present study examines whether portfolio benefits observed in major markets translate to highly developed Small Open Economies (SOEs) settings and whether protection in crises is systematic or episodic across countries. We examine twelve highly developed Small Open Economies (SOEs) countries using daily equity returns and a global green bond index over 2014-2023, with explicit crisis windows for COVID-19 and the Russia-Ukraine war. The design separates normal-time hedging from crisis-time shifts through interaction terms and evaluates reliability with country-level OLS and HAC (Newey-West) errors to accommodate daily-data features (Newey & West, 1987). This approach recognizes that market microstructure and policy frameworks can generate heterogeneous cross-asset linkages that pooled specifications may mask (Baur & Lucey, 2010;Baur & McDermott, 2010;Reboredo, 2018).

The hypotheses are stated to allow clear acceptance or rejection of the empirical results and conclusion:  H 1 (Hedging in normal times). In non-crisis periods, green bond returns exhibit non-positive average co-movement with national equity returns in the sample countries (baseline coefficient on green bond returns ≤ 0). Diversification implies zero or negative conditional linkage in tranquil conditions (Baur & McDermott, 2010;Reboredo, 2018).  H 2a (Safe haven -COVID-19). During the COVID-19 window, the green bond-equity linkage becomes more negative relative to non-crisis periods (crisis-interaction coefficient ≤ 0). Safe-haven behavior requires decoupling or inverse co-movement under systemic stress (Baur & Lucey, 2010).  H 2b (Safe haven -Russia-Ukraine war). During the Russia-Ukraine war window, the green bond-equity linkage becomes more negative relative to non-crisis periods (crisis-interaction coefficient ≤ 0). This hypothesis highlights if green bonds provide protection in geopolitical shocks, crisis interactions should be non-positive.  H 3 (Robustness to crisis dating). The conclusions for H 2a persist under an alternative COVID-19 start date, 1 February 2020 rather than 11 March 2020. It is tested whether coefficient signs and significance levels remain unaffected.

If the baseline green-bond coefficient is significantly ≤ 0 (panel and/or OLS), accept H 1 for that country Otherwise if > 0 or insignificant, do not accept H 1 . If a crisis-interaction term is significantly ≤ 0, accept H 2a or H 2b as applicable; If a crisis-interaction term is significantly > 0 or insignificant, do not accept. -If alternative COVID dating leaves signs or significance materially unchanged, accept H 3 otherwise, do not accept H 3 . By tying conclusions to these pre-specified criteria, the analysis clarifies where and when green bonds provide diversification and whether crisis protection is persistent or context-dependent across highly developed Small Open Economies (SOEs) markets. This approach may have practical implications for allocation and policy. For investors, green bonds in highly developed Small Open Economies (SOEs) markets should be treated as conditional diversifiers, with country-specific risk budgets and rebalancing rules informed by baseline linkages and crisis shifts. For policymakers, strengthening verification, reporting, and secondary-market liquidity can support stable co-movement properties and mitigate greenwashing-related pricing distortions that may otherwise undermine the risk-management role of labeled debt (Reboredo & Ugolini, 2020;Ferrer et al., 2021).

Rather than deploying a broad, non-specific 'non-G20' classification that risks conflating divergent stages of economic development, this study explicitly stratifies its twelve-nation sample around the well-established framework of highly developed Small Open Economies (SOEs). The sample includes several Western European nations-specifically Belgium, Denmark, Finland, the Netherlands, Norway, and Sweden-which, despite possessing deep domestic financial institutions and advanced capital markets, operate structurally outside the systemic core of G20 economic governance. In international macro-finance, highly developed SOEs face unique vulnerabilities; they are highly integrated into global trade and financial networks, yet they lack the massive domestic market depth or dominant sovereign currency-issuance networks necessary to dictate international liquidity conditions (Lane & Milesi-Ferretti, 2007). During periods of global market distress, these countries are intensely susceptible to cross-border capital reallocation and rapid liquidity withdrawals (Baur & McDermott, 2010). Isolating these advanced but structurally exposed nations provides an ideal testing ground to observe whether green bonds offer localized, autonomous portfolio insulation or if their hedging capacity is entirely subordinate to global cross-asset contagion channels. The sample covers the period 2014-2023. The starting point is determined by the earliest date on which both the national equity price indices and the global green bond index are available at a continuous daily frequency, while the endpoint is set prior to late-2023 market developments to preserve a stable evaluation window. All-time series are harmonized to a common business-day calendar; non-trading days are excluded rather than forward-filled so as to avoid inducing spurious serial correlation. Returns are computed from price (as opposed to total-return) indices in order to eliminate cross-country dividend-timing effects that could contaminate high-frequency co-movements. Data cleaning is deliberately conservative: only in the presence of diagnostic evidence of extreme, glitch-related outliers is light tail winsorization applied, thereby attenuating the influence of obvious recording errors without suppressing genuine market shocks.

Descriptive statistics (mean, standard deviation, skewness, kurtosis, and sample sizes) are reported in the Appendix to document distributional features and to motivate the use of heteroskedasticity-and autocorrelation-robust inference. Let P i,t denote the equity price index level for country I on day t, and P t GB he level of the global green bond index on day t. We compute daily log returns as: Multiplying by 100 expresses the returns in percent (so a value of 0.50 equals +0.5% for that day). Log returns are standard in high-frequency work: they add conveniently over time and behave approximately normally for daily horizons. To assess whether the green bond-equity linkage changes during crises, two event indicators are employed: In robustness analysis, the COVID onset is advanced to 1 February 2020 to allow for pre-announcement repricing.

We model the conditional linkage between national equity returns and the global green bond index using a fixed-effects panel with crisis interactions: where r i,t is the daily log return (percent) on the price-index equity benchmark for country I at date t and r t GB is the daily log return (percent) on the global green bond index, whereas 1 COVID , t equals 1 from 11 March 2020 onward and 0 otherwise , and 1 WAR,t equals 1 from 24 February 2022 onward and 0 otherwise. The error term ε i,t captures idiosyncratic shocks. Estimation is by within-country (fixed-effects) OLS with heteroskedasticity-and autocorrelation-consistent (HAC/Newey-West) standard errors. The α i are country fixed effects (country-specific intercepts) that absorb time-invariant differences across markets-e.g., structural features of market depth, regulation, taxation, or investor composition-so that slope estimates are not confounded by persistent cross-country heterogeneity. The coefficient β measures the baseline (non-crisis) co-movement between green bonds and equities.When both crisis indicators are zero, a 1 percentage-point move in the green-bond return is associated, on average, with beta (β) percentage points in the equity return of country i. The coefficients γ cov and γ war capture crisis-period shifts in that linkage..During the COVID-19 window the conditional slope becomes β+γ cov, , and during the Russia-Ukraine window it becomes β+γ war . Hence, γ<0 indicates that equities co-move less with green bonds (or more inversely) in the corresponding crisis (a more protective relation), while γ>0indicates that the relation tightens (protection erodes). Because the α i partial out level differences, inference concerns co-movements rather than mean returns, aligning the specification with hedge/safe-haven concepts that are defined in terms of conditional correlations/slopes. The summarization of the decision rules on our hypotheses is as follows To ensure the internal validity of our panel parameters, the empirical design explicitly addresses potential endogeneity and bidirectional feedback loops. A common concern in equity-bond panel frameworks is that localized domestic equity shocks could simultaneously trigger portfolio rebalancing that alters the demand and pricing of fixed-income instruments.

To insulate our model from this reverse-causality channel, we utilize a global green bond index as our key independent variable rather than country-specific components. Following systemic asset-pricing frameworks (Bekaert et al., 2011), global financial factors operate as structurally exogenous metrics relative to individual small open economies. Because the global green bond pricing structure is fundamentally driven by multi-billion-dollar aggregate institutional flows and macro-issuances across major currency blocs (Reboredo & Ugolini, 2020), localized equity shocks within individual nations in our sample (e.g., Cyprus, Iceland, or Finland) lack the market scale to retroactively impact the global index. Consequently, the reverse-causal transmission pathway from national equity returns to global green bond performance is mathematically and structurally negligible, satisfying the exogeneity criteria required for consistent fixed-effects panel estimations (Gormley & Matsa, 2014).

 Estimator: We use within-country (fixed-effects) OLS. This method subtracts each country's average over time, so stable country traits (that we cannot observe directly) do not bias the estimated co-movements.  Standard errors: Daily financial returns often have heteroskedasticity (variance changes over time) and serial correlation (today's shock leaks into tomorrow). We therefore compute HAC (Newey-West) standard errors so that our p-values remain valid under these conditions.  Country-level robustness: To make sure pooled results are not driven by one or two large markets, we also estimate the same regression separately for each country (simple OLS with HAC errors). If country-level results match the panel patterns (signs and significance), our conclusions are not an artifact of pooling.  Alternative COVID start: We shift the COVID dummy to 1 February 2020 (earlier onset) and re-estimate to check whether conclusions survive reasonable changes in event dating.

 Fixed effects give each country its own baseline level (intercept) so that structural, time-invariant differences-like regulatory regimes or investor composition-do not contaminate the estimated co-movement.  Interactions with crisis dummies let the slope (the green bond-equity linkage) change during crises. This is precisely what the hedge vs. safe-haven taxonomy requires: an asset might look helpful in quiet times but behave differently when stress hits.

Dynamic conditional correlations provide an indication regarding the extent to which national equities and green bonds move together over time, highlighting state dependence (correlations can turn more or less positive across regimes). The panel regressions then test hypotheses about those co-movements: the baseline slope beta (β) evaluates hedging in normal conditions (H 1 ), while the interaction terms γ cov and γ war assess crisis-time shifts in COVID-19 and the Russia-Ukraine windows (H 2a /H 2b ). Examining the simultaneous movements of these variables allows us to see whether descriptive patterns in DCC (e.g., low or negative average correlations, wide swings) translate into statistically credible hedging or safe-haven behavior once unobserved country heterogeneity is controlled for.

DCC correlations cluster at low positive levels, consistent with modest integration in typical conditions. The panel, however, detects a negative and statistically significant baseline linkage (β=-0.996, p=.003) indicating hedging in calm periods (H 1 accepted). During COVID-19, the slope shifts positive (γ cov =+1.021, p=.008), and in the war window it is marginally positive (γ war =+0.448, p=.066) implying an erosion of protection under stress (H 2a /H 2b not accepted). Economically, the calm-period elasticity, ≈1% countermovement for a 1% green-bond move, is substantial, but it does not persist in crises.

DCC averages are weakly positive, indicating limited routine diversification. The panel aligns with this: the baseline is not a hedge (β=+0.118, p=.644) H 1 is not accepted. The COVID shift is positive and marginal (γ cov =+0.558, p=.054) again inconsistent with a haven in the pandemic. By contrast, the war-time shift is negative and significant (γ war =-0.517, p=.005), showing episode-specific decoupling (H 2b accepted). Thus, protection is contingent on the shock, not a general feature.

DCC means hover near zero with a wide range (strongly negative minima and moderately positive maxima), signaling a flip-flop correlation through time. The panel registers an insignificant negative baseline (β=-0.356, p=.202), consistent with weak hedging (H 1 partially supported). COVID induces a positive and significant shift (γcov=+0.865, p=.006) H 2a not accepted, while the war shift is negative and marginal (γ war =-0.380, p=.060), suggesting selective protection in the geopolitical episode (H 2b accepted, marginal).

DCC indicates a persistently positive alignment (higher mean, narrow range), implying limited scope for diversification. The panel mirrors this: no baseline hedging (β=+0.180, p=.565) H 1 not accepted and no significant crisis-time adjustments (COVID p=.150, warp=.690) H 2a /H 2b .Green bonds appear integrated with Danish equities across states.

DCC averages are low positive, but the panel reveals a large negative baseline (β=-0.973, p=.002), consistent with strong hedging in tranquil periods (H 1 accepted). The COVID shift is strongly positive (γcov=+1.338, p<.001), indicating that the calm-period benefit does not carry into the pandemic (H 2a not accepted). The war interaction is negligible (γ war =+0.054, p=.813) so H 2b not accepted.

DCC suggests weak integration. The panel baseline is negative but imprecise (β=-0.522, p=.194), implying diversification rather than a reliably negative slope, H 1 is partially supported. Crisis interactions are positive but insignificant (COVID p=.148; war p=.271), so there is no systematic crisis shift is detected (H 2a /H 2b not accepted).

DCC averages are low positive with variability across time. The panel baseline is negative but insignificant (β=-0.349, p=.365), consistent with weak hedging; H 1 is partially supported. In COVID, the slope tightens (γ cov =+0.995, p=.023), which suggests that H 2a is not accepted, whereas the war shift is negative but also insignificant (γ war =-0.422, p=.129) and H 2b is not accepted. Netting these findings, green bonds do not provide reliable crisis protection. Iceland DCC indicates small, near-zero average correlations. The panel shows no baseline hedging (β=+0.066, p=.824); H 1 not accepted and no significant crisis adjustments (COVID p=.449; warp=.243p). Both H 2a /H 2b are not accepted. Green bonds behave largely orthogonally to Icelandic equities, but without systematic decoupling in crises.

DCC spans a wide interval (negative to positive), reflecting strong state dependence. The panel baseline is negative and significant (β=-0.854, p=.008), supporting hedging in calm periods therefore H 1 is accepted. Both crisis interactions are positive and significant (γ cov =+0.989, p=.006, ,γ war =+0.611, p=.008), implying loss of protection in stress H 2a /H 2b not accepted. In this country, although the statistical significance is shown to be within our criteria, the positives baselines differ from our original hypotheses; therefore, a "hedge-but-not-haven" pattern aligns with the wide DCC range.

DCC averages are low, consistent with weak integration. The panel baseline is negative and significant (β=-0.772, p=.017), indicating calm-period hedging H 1 accepted. COVID brings a positive and significant shift (γ cov =+0.980, p=.007), H 2a not accepted, while the war shift is insignificant (γ war =+0.280, p=.230), H 2b not accepted. Norway DCC shows a negative mean correlation, consistent with routine hedging. The panel confirms a negative and significant baseline (β=-0.720, p=.018) H 1 accepted. The COVID shift is small and imprecise (p=.500, and the war shift is marginally positive (p=.095), providing no robust evidence of crisis-time improvement or deterioration (H 2a /H 2b not accepted). The selection of our twelve-country sample relies on an intentional stratification balancing institutional development and sovereign policy scale. While the sample features highly advanced, liquid, and innovative Western European economies (e.g., Sweden, Denmark, Norway, Finland, the Netherlands, and Belgium), these markets are structurally categorized as Small Open Economies (SOEs) positioned outside the immediate G20 financial-governance framework. Lacking the massive domestic market scale and systemic currency-issuance networks of G20 superpowers, these nations exhibit a distinct structural vulnerability to cross-border capital flights and global funding shocks, making them a crucial testing ground for whether green bonds can provide autonomous localized insulation during global crises. Taken together, the DCC evidence and the panel estimates indicate that the equity-green bond linkage in highly developed Small Open Economies (SOEs) markets is state-contingent and heterogeneous, rather than uniform across countries or crises. Descriptively, average DCC correlations cluster near zero, with wide ranges in several markets, signaling that the direction and strength of co-movement can change materially over time. The panel formalizes that intuition: a subset of countries exhibits statistically and economically meaningful negative baselines (β<0\beta<0β<0)-notably Sweden, Belgium, Finland, Israel, the Netherlands, and Norway-consistent with acceptance of H1 (hedging in normal conditions). These elasticities are non-trivial at daily frequency: a 1% move in the global green-bond index associates with roughly 0.7-1.1 percentage points of opposite (or near-zero) movement in national equities. By contrast, several markets show weak diversification (negative but imprecise β\betaβ) or no hedging (non-negative β\betaβ), which aligns with DCC profiles that are either persistently positive (e.g., Denmark) or close to zero but narrow. In short, routine risk-smoothing is available but selective, depending on the market.

Crisis behavior is even more differentiated. During the COVID-19 window, many countries display positive and significant crisis shifts (γcov>0), implying that the calm-period hedge eroded or reversed under pandemic stress. This is consistent with the DCC ranges that widen markedly around 2020 and with plausible mechanisms: (i) liquidity strains that compress cross-asset differences as investors liquidate credit (including labeled green bonds) alongside equities; (ii) flight-to-quality within fixed income into the safest sovereigns, which can raise the beta of diversified bond indices relative to risky assets; and (iii) benchmark composition effects, since global green-bond indices are tilted toward investment-grade credit with non-trivial spread risk that can comove with equities in systemic sell-offs. Consequently, H2a cannot be upheld in general even for countries with strong calm-period hedging (e.g., Sweden, Belgium, Finland): the negative baseline does not translate into crisis insulation during the pandemic. The Russia-Ukraine episode produces a more market-specific pattern. A small number of countries (e.g., Cyprus, and marginally the Czech Republic) exhibit negative war-time shifts (γwar<0), suggesting episode-contingent decoupling, while others (e.g., Sweden, Israel, Belgium) experience positive shifts that tighten co-movement, and several show no material change. This dispersion likely reflects differences in investor base and market microstructure (depth, local vs. global participants), exposure of domestic equities to sectors sensitive to rates and spreads, and indirect geopolitical channels (energy prices, regional risk premia). The DCC minima and maxima are consistent with such variety: in some market's correlations turn sharply negative in specific windows, in others they remain durably positive. Accordingly, H2b can be accepted only selectively and does not characterize the cross-section as a whole.

From a portfolio perspective, the results support a conditional-diversifier view of green bonds in highly developed Small Open Economies (SOEs) contexts. In markets with accepted H1, introducing green bonds alongside equities is expected to lower day-to-day variance without eliminating equity beta; however, the pandemic-era tightening cautions against relying on green bonds as a stand-alone safe haven. Crisis-time protection, where present (e.g., Cyprus in the war window), appears episodic and market-dependent rather than systematic. For tactical allocation, this implies (i) country-specific tilts-not a uniform allocation rule across highly developed Small Open Economies (SOEs) markets; (ii) complementing green bonds with traditional safe assets (high-grade sovereigns, duration, or gold) when drawdown protection is the priority; and (iii) state-aware monitoring, given that the same market can switch from negative to positive co-movement across regimes. The findings are robust to reasonable variations in event dating (advancing the COVID onset to 1 February 2020) and to estimation at the country level with HAC-robust inference: signs and significance remain qualitatively unchanged in the vast majority of cases, indicating that pooled inferences are not artifacts of averaging and that results are not sensitive to a narrow definition of the pandemic window. Two caveats qualify external validity. First, the green-bond series is a global index; while appropriate for investable exposure, it may imperfectly match country-specific issuance or local green-credit conditions. Second, the analysis focuses on daily returns; although well-suited to measuring co-movement, daily frequency can understate slower-moving channels (e.g., reporting-cycle effects or gradual repricing of climate policy risk). These limitations do not overturn the conclusions but suggest avenues for future work (e.g., incorporating local green-bond segments or multi-horizon models).

In aggregate, the cross-country evidence affirms that hedging in normal conditions is real but selective, while safe-haven performance is neither uniform nor persistent across crises. This state-contingent heterogeneity-visible in both DCC dynamics and regression-based shifts-underscores the importance of market-specific assessment and regime-aware portfolio design when green bonds are used to enhance resilience in highly developed Small Open Economies (SOEs) equity allocations.

Our empirical findings reveal that green bonds operate as conditional diversifiers rather than invariant safe havens. The presence of statistically significant, negative baseline slopes during tranquil periods confirms that green bonds act as effective hedging instruments under routine market conditions. This normal-time decoupling aligns with the asset-pricing view that pro-environmental mandates generate a stable, long-horizon investor base ('greenium' stickiness), keeping these assets insulated from everyday equity volatility (Zerbib, 2019;Flammer, 2021). However, the systemic positive shifts observed during the COVID-19 pandemic demonstrate that this protection is highly state-dependent. Rather than acting as a traditional safe haven (Baur & Lucey, 2010), green bonds experienced an erosion of their hedging capacity, collapsing into positive co-movements with equities during peak stress.

Two foundational economic mechanisms explain this crisis-time erosion of protection. First, in line with the liquidity-spiral framework formalized by Brunnermeier and Pedersen (2009), extreme systemic shocks trigger generalized funding constraints. Institutional asset managers facing margin calls or redemptions are forced to liquidate liquid fixed-income assets uniformly-regardless of their 'green' credentials-compressing cross-asset differences and driving up correlations. Second, benchmark composition risk plays a dominant role. Global green bond indices are heavily weighted toward investment-grade corporate issuers rather than risk-free sovereign duration (Ferrer et al., 2021). During broad funding crises, corporate credit spreads widen in tandem with falling equity prices. This credit risk component overrides any underlying duration-driven flight-to-quality benefit, causing green bonds to trade like generic spread products during global market drawdowns. Conversely, the highly fragmented, market-specific reactions seen during the Russia-Ukraine conflict underscore that geopolitical shocks transmit differently than pandemic shocks. Geopolitical stress does not trigger a uniform global liquidity squeeze; instead, it reallocates capital based on regional trade linkages, energy dependencies, and localized risk premia, explaining why decoupling occurred only selectively.

p.s: Portfolio Allocation in Small Open Economies
p.t: The evidence supports treating green bonds as conditional diversifiers rather than universal safe havens, but the feasibility and strength of those benefits depend critically on market development and issuance depth. In countries with limited local green-bond supply, shallow secondary-market liquidity, or a concentrated issuer base, investors face higher implementation risk (wider bid-ask spreads, slippage), greater tracking error versus global benchmarks, and a higher probability that diversification gains in calm periods will not persist in stress. Where no meaningful domestic ESG fixed-income segment exists, allocations must typically rely on global or regional green-bond indices (or on sovereign and supranational green issues) rather than purely domestic bond issuance; this introduces currency and hedging costs, benchmark-composition exposure (e.g., to investment-grade credit spreads), and potential mismatch between local equity risk and external fixed-income dynamics. For institutional asset allocation within developed SOEs, these findings carry critical tactical implications. Because these nations are highly exposed to global capital flows but lack the scale to anchor global liquidity (Lane & Milesi-Ferretti, 2007), a strategic green bond sleeve will successfully reduce everyday portfolio variance but will fail as a standalone crisis buffer. Asset managers cannot treat green credit as a substitute for canonical safe assets. To maintain capital preservation during systemic drawdowns, green bond allocations must be explicitly paired with unbundled sovereign duration, cash, or gold. In sum, the portfolio value of green bonds hinges not only on the sign and stability of the equity linkage but also on the market microstructure that delivers the exposure. Where ESG/green fixed-income markets are underdeveloped, diversification benefits are harder to capture consistently and should be complemented with traditional safe assets and explicit crisis-time risk controls.

The results indicate that the risk properties of green bonds are state-contingent rather than invariant, which has direct implications for prudential design, market architecture, and public issuance policy in highly developed Small Open Economies (SOEs) markets. In tranquil periods, green bonds often deliver diversification benefits; in systemic stress-particularly during the COVID-19 shock-co-movements with equities can tighten, tempering any presumption of automatic crisis insulation. Policy frames that treat labeled credit as uniformly stabilizing therefore risk overstating its buffer role in downturns (Brunnermeier & Pedersen, 2009, on liquidity spirals;Krishnamurthy & Vissing-Jorgensen, 2012, on flight-to-quality).For central banks and macroprudential supervisors, these results challenge the regulatory assumption that sustainable financial instruments are inherently stabilizing assets. Eligibility and haircut calibrations within central bank collateral frameworks must remain strictly risk-sensitive, anchored primarily on basic credit and liquidity parameters rather than green labels (Baur & McDermott, 2010). To prevent procyclicality during future market disruptions, policies should focus on structural market depth: harmonizing disclosure frameworks (such as the ICMA Green Bond Principles), expanding local-currency sovereign green issuance to build benchmark yield curves, and diversifying the domestic institutional investor base to absorb sudden order imbalances during global cross-asset liquidations. Market depth, transparency, and credibility. The stabilizing potential of green bonds depends critically on secondary-market depth and information quality. Policies that (a) consolidate disclosure around the ICMA Green Bond Principles (ICMA, 2018/2021), (b) promote credible external reviews/certification (e.g., Climate Bonds Initiative standards), and (c) harmonize taxonomies (to reduce cross-border frictions) can lower information asymmetry and liquidity premia, thereby improving diversification properties in normal times and reducing the odds that green bonds trade like generic spread products in stress (Climate Bonds Initiative, 2023; Reboredo & Ugolini, 2020). The "greenium" literature underscores why credibility matters: where greenness is well documented and trusted, pricing premia arise and persist; where greenwashing risks are salient, premia compress or vanish (Zerbib, 2019;Larcker & Watts, 2020;Flammer, 2021). Strengthening reporting around use-of-proceeds and impacts directly addresses that credibility channel.

The crisis patterns we document are consistent with the fact that global green-bond indices are tilted to investment-grade credit; in broad funding shocks, spread risk often co-moves with equities (Ferrer et al., 2021;Reboredo, 2018). Policy can mitigate this structural linkage by encouraging a more diversified issuer base (e.g., a mix of sovereign/supranational/agency and high-quality corporate supply), and by supporting market-making (e.g., primary dealer obligations in sovereign green lines, repo eligibility) to keep bid-ask spreads orderly in stress. A more balanced benchmark mix (duration, sector, and currency) reduces the likelihood that a single risk factor (credit spreads) dominates co-movement in crises. Sovereign and sub-sovereign issuance strategy. For highly developed Small Open Economies (SOEs) markets with thin domestic ESG fixed-income universes, sovereign green programs can anchor market development-ideally with regular calendars, benchmark-size lines, and tap reopenings to build depth and on-the-run liquidity. Robust allocation and reporting practices (e.g., ICMA-aligned frameworks, third-party verification, granular impact metrics) help sustain investor demand and lower issuance premia over time (ICMA, 2018(ICMA, /2021;;Climate Bonds Initiative, 2023). Where feasible, local-currency green issuance reduces FX-hedging frictions for domestic buyers and can align the risk properties of green bonds more closely with domestic equities, potentially moderating co-movement in stress. At the same time, authorities should avoid over-reliance on short or clustered maturities that could concentrate rollover risk during volatile episodes.

Investor base diversification and microstructure. A broader, stickier investor base-mixing long-horizon domestic institutions with international ESG-dedicated funds-tends to reduce order-imbalance amplification in selloffs (Brunnermeier & Pedersen, 2009). Regulatory nudges that facilitate mandate clarity for ESG allocations (without soft guarantees of safety) and support transparent, low-cost trading venues can improve turnover and price discovery, limiting the conditions under which green bonds behave like high-beta spread products. Evidence that green premia depend on investor composition (e.g., retail vs. institutional demand) reinforces the point that who holds the bonds matters for risk behavior (see the cross-market findings summarized in Zerbib, 2019; and recent regional evidence discussed by Ferrer et al., 2021). Green labels, taxonomies, or purchase tilts do not guarantee safe-haven performance. In line with previous research (Baur & Lucey, 2010;Baur & McDermott, 2010) our results suggest that any prudential or operational treatment should be risk-sensitive, anchored in the same credit, liquidity, and duration diagnostics applied to conventional bonds, and complemented by market-structure improvements (transparency, market-making, investor-base diversification) that make hedging benefits more reliable across states.

First, event-dating sensitivity is addressed by advancing the COVID-19 onset to 1 February 2020; the signs and statistical significance of the key coefficients-baseline slopes β\betaβ (H1) and crisis interactions γcov\gamma_{\mathrm{cov}}γcov, γwar\gamma_{\mathrm{war}}γwar (H2a/H2b)-remain qualitatively unchanged, indicating that conclusions do not hinge on a narrow definition of the pandemic window. Second, estimation design is stress-tested by re-estimating the specification country by country using OLS with HAC (Newey-West) standard errors; the concordance in signs and significance with the pooled fixed-effects (FE) results rules out the possibility that findings are artifacts of cross-sectional pooling (Newey & West, 1987).

p.s: Serial correlation, heteroskedasticity, and cross-sectional dependence.
p.t: Daily returns typically exhibit conditional heteroskedasticity and short-run serial correlation; HAC inference mitigates these concerns in both pooled and country regressions (Newey & West, 1987). However, cross-sectional dependencee.g., common shocks or region-wide risk factorscan bias standard FE errors if strong. While country-level OLS attenuates pooling concerns, future work could deploy Driscoll-Kraay Ses (robust to very general cross-sectional and temporal dependence) or common correlated effects estimators to absorb unobserved common factors (Driscoll & Kraay, 1998;Pesaran, 2006).

The crisis effects are identified via sharp dummies (WHO declaration; invasion date). This design estimates average slope shifts within each window; it does not trace intra-window dynamics (e.g., early-panic vs. late-adjustment phases) nor allow for multiple breaks. As a complement, endogenous break tests (Bai & Perron, 2003) could assess whether additional structural shifts exist in the slope process, and time-varying parameter or Markov-switching models could capture regime persistence and transitions (Hamilton, 1989). Distributional and outlier robustness. The return construction (log differences, percent scale) and conservative tail winsorization limit the influence of recording glitches while preserving genuine shocks. Still, estimates can be sensitive to extreme drawdowns concentrated in short intervals. As further insurance, influence diagnostics (e.g., DFITS, leave-one-week-out re-estimation) or M-estimators could be reported; if results persist, this strengthens claims of distributional robustness (White, 1980).

The green-bond factor is a global index-appropriate for investable exposure but imperfect as a proxy for country-specific issuance or local ESG credit conditions. This raises two issues. First, benchmark-composition risk (credit-spread and duration tilt) may account for part of the crisis co-movement (Ferrer, Shahzad, & Soriano, 2021;Reboredo, 2018). Second, currency and hedging matter: a USD-or EUR-denominated global index may embed FX dynamics not aligned with local equity risk. Sensitivity to (i) alternative green-bond indices (e.g., Bloomberg MSCI, S&P, ICE), (ii) hedged vs. unhedged versions where available, and (iii) local or regional green segments where data permit, would refine external validity. Complementary DCC-GARCH estimates (Engle, 2002) already indicate state dependence in correlations; aligning those dynamics with index composition would illuminate mechanisms.

The daily horizon is well suited to co-movement and short-horizon hedging but cannot capture slow-moving channels-dividend policy, reporting cycles, policy-driven repricing, or issuance-depth effects-that unfold at weekly/monthly frequencies. Multi-horizon estimators (e.g., mixed-frequency regressions, MIDAS) or an aggregation analysis (daily → weekly → monthly) would test whether the hedge/safe-haven inferences persist once microstructure noise is averaged out.

The interaction design presumes linear slope shifts conditional on a crisis dummy. Yet safe-haven behavior is often threshold-dependent: protection may emerge beyond a volatility or drawdown threshold. Extensions using smooth transition or threshold models (Hansen, 1999), quantile regressions, or state variables (e.g., VIX-style proxies, credit-spread levels) interacted with green-bond returns could uncover latent nonlinearity obscured by average crisis dummies.

Country-by-country estimation yields a panel of ppp-values across three focal parameters; even with consistent signs, nominal significance can be inflated by multiple comparisons. Reporting false discovery rate adjusted qqq-values (Benjamini & Hochberg, 1995) or Romano-Wolf step-down adjustments would bolster inferential discipline without materially changing conclusions if effects are strong. Economic vs. statistical significance. Throughout, the discussion reports elasticities (equity percentage-point response per 1% green-bond move) to anchor portfolio relevance. A full variance-decomposition or out-of-sample risk exercise (e.g., realized volatility reduction in equity-green mixes with/without green bonds) would further quantify economic significance and test whether the negative baselines translate into ex ante risk control once transaction costs and liquidity are considered. Scope and external validity. The evidence pertains to twelve highly developed Small Open Economies (SOEs) markets over 2014-late-2023. External validity is strongest for markets with similar issuance depth, investor base, and regulatory structures. In countries with nascent ESG fixed-income segments, investability constraints (small free float, discontinuous trading) may weaken the link between statistical co-movement and implementable hedges. Conversely, in larger markets with active sovereign/supranational green issuance, the behavior may more closely resemble high-grade credit with deeper liquidity and more reliable diversification in calm states. Unmodeled channels and endogeneity. Finally, while fixed effects absorb time-invariant heterogeneity, time-varying omitted factors-e.g., synchronized monetary shocks, energy-price spikes, or local policy announcements-could affect both equities and green bonds. Augmenting the specification with global/Regional controls (Treasury returns, IG spread indexes, oil), or employing instrumented designs where plausible instruments exist, would test whether the hedge/safe-haven coefficients are robust to common-shock controls.

Within these limits, the core inferences-selective negative baselines consistent with hedging (H1) and non-systematic safe-haven shifts in crises (H2a/H2b)-prove robust to the event-dating and estimation checks implemented here. The additional diagnostics outlined above would further tighten identification and generalizability without altering the central message: in highly developed Small Open Economies (SOEs) markets, green bonds act as conditional diversifiers whose crisis behavior is regime-and market-dependent rather than uniformly safe-haven-like.

This study assessed whether labelled green bonds hedged national equities in normal conditions and whether they acted as safe havens during crises in twelve highly developed Small Open Economies (SOEs) markets over 2014-late 2023. Using daily data, dynamic-correlation diagnostics, and a fixed-effects panel that separated baseline co-movement from crisis-state shifts (COVID-19 and the Russia-Ukraine episode), and corroborating the pooled estimates with country-level OLS under HAC inference, the analysis yielded a clear set of results. Hedging in normal times proved present but selective. Several markets exhibited negative and statistically meaningful baseline slopes, thereby supporting H 1 in those cases. Elsewhere, baselines were weakly negative or near zero, indicating at most diversification rather than a reliably negative linkage. At the daily horizon, the magnitudes were economically non-trivial: green-bond moves were associated with counter-or near-zero equity responses large enough to smooth routine variance, though not to replicate canonical safe assets. The pattern that green bonds hedge equities in tranquil periods but do not constitute a universal safe haven under stress is consistent with prior evidence that situates green bonds close to high-quality sovereign and investment-grade corporate debt in risk characteristics. The frequent pandemic-era tightening accords with findings that labeled credit can co-move with risky assets during broad funding shocks, while the heterogeneous war-time responses echo results in that safe-haven properties are episodic and market-dependent. The present study extends this evidence base by documenting these behaviors in twelve highly developed Small Open Economies (SOEs) markets and by separating normal-time hedging from crisis-time shifts using an explicit interaction framework. Turning to crisis, the evidence did not support a universal safe-haven characterization. During the pandemic window, crisis interactions were frequently positive and significant, implying tighter equity-green-bond co-movement relative to baseline; as a result, H 2a was not accepted at the aggregate level. During the Russia-Ukraine window, estimated shifts varied across markets, yielding selective acceptance of H2b in a limited number of cases and no uniform pattern otherwise. Read alongside the dynamic-correlation ranges, these findings indicated that green-bond protection was state-contingent and episode-specific rather than systematic.

Robustness was assessed along two dimensions. When the start of the COVID-19 window was advanced to 1 February 2020, the signs and statistical significance of the key parameters remained materially unchanged. In addition, re-estimation at the country level using OLS with HAC standard errors yielded coefficients that aligned in sign and, in most cases, in significance with the pooled fixed-effects results. Taking these outcomes together, is justifying the acceptance of H 3 , indicating that the study's conclusions did not hinge on the precise dating of the pandemic onset nor on the use of a pooled panel. Methodologically, the study distinguished routine from crisis-conditional co-movement within a single empirical framework and verified that pooled inferences persisted at the country level. Substantively, the results positioned green bonds in highly developed Small Open Economies (SOEs) markets as conditional diversifiers: they reduced day-to-day equity risk in several countries under normal conditions, yet they did not deliver uniform insulation in systemic stress, with crisis performance depending on the market and the episode.
